questions.prompt: Which datasheet number most directly tells you the small-signal bandwidth you'll get for a closed-loop gain of \(G\)?
options: The slew rate
The gain-bandwidth product (bandwidth \(\approx GBW/G\) for a non-inverting gain \(G\))
The input offset voltage
The input resistance
questions.explanation: For a single-pole op-amp, closed-loop bandwidth \(\approx f\cdot f_u=GBW/G_{noninv}\). Slew rate limits LARGE signals; offset and input resistance are DC specs.

questions.prompt: The ADA4891 lists an open-loop gain of 66 dB. What is that as a ratio (V/V)?
questions.explanation: \(10^{66/20}=10^{3.3}=1995\). Only about 2000: a fast CMOS op-amp trades DC gain for speed, so gain errors are larger than with a 100+ dB part.

questions.prompt: The ADA4891's input common-mode range is \(-V_s-0.3\ \mathrm{V}\) to \(+V_s-0.8\ \mathrm{V}\). On \(\pm5\ \mathrm{V}\) supplies (\(V_s=5\ \mathrm{V}\)), what is the highest input voltage that keeps it working properly, in V?
questions.explanation: \(+V_s-0.8=5-0.8=4.2\ \mathrm{V}\). The inputs can go slightly below the negative rail (\(-5.3\ \mathrm{V}\)) but not to the positive one. A follower with a 4.5 V input would misbehave even though it is inside the supplies.

questions.prompt: With the ADA4891 at gain 10, you want a 1 V-peak sine at 20 MHz. Which limit matters?
options: Bandwidth: 20 MHz is close to the 24 MHz closed-loop corner (gain already down ~2 dB); the slew need of 126 V/µs is within 170 V/µs
Slew rate: 126 V/µs exceeds 170 V/µs
Neither: 20 MHz is far below 240 MHz
Offset voltage
questions.explanation: Slew: \(2\pi\times20\ \mathrm{MHz}\times1\ \mathrm{V}=126\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}<170\) ✔. Bandwidth: the closed-loop pole is at 24 MHz, so at 20 MHz \(|H|=10/\sqrt{1+(20/24)^2}=7.7\) (−2.3 dB). Comparing 20 MHz with the 240 MHz GBW forgets that gain 10 divides it.

questions.prompt: With the ADA4891 at gain 2 (240 MHz GBW, so 120 MHz bandwidth), you need a 2 V-peak sine at 30 MHz. What happens?
options: It works fine; 30 MHz is far below the 120 MHz bandwidth
It is bandwidth-limited to −3 dB
The offset voltage clips it
It slew-limits: the sine needs \(2\pi\times30\ \mathrm{MHz}\times2\ \mathrm{V}=377\ \mathrm{V/\mu s}\), more than 170 V/µs, even though 30 MHz is well inside the 120 MHz bandwidth
questions.explanation: Bandwidth is fine (30 ≪ 120 MHz), but the slope needed exceeds SR, so the output distorts toward a triangle. Gotcha: a big GBW doesn't guarantee large-signal speed; check SR separately.

questions.prompt: The reader compares the fastest Analog Devices op-amps (GHz GBW, slew rates near \(1\ \mathrm{GV/s}\)) with ultra-low-power parts (sub-µA supply current). What trade-off do these tables show?
options: Faster op-amps always use less power
Power consumption doesn't depend on speed
Speed (GBW and slew rate) costs supply current: the fastest parts draw tens of mA, while sub-µA parts are very slow
Low-power parts have higher slew rates
questions.explanation: Slew rate \(\approx I_{max}/C_x\) and GBW \(\approx G_m/C_x\) both need bias current to charge internal capacitances quickly. That's why IoT/sensor op-amps sacrifice speed, and GHz op-amps burn power (reader Sec. 18.6). Read the supply-current line next to the speed specs.

questions.prompt: Preview of CMRR. The ADA4891 lists CMRR = 88 dB. Treat it as: a 1 V change of both inputs together looks like a differential input error of \(1\ \mathrm{V}/\mathrm{CMRR}\). How big is that equivalent input error, in µV?
questions.explanation: \(\mathrm{CMRR}=10^{88/20}=2.51\times10^4\). Equivalent error \(=\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{V}}{2.51\times10^4}=39.81\ \mu\mathrm{V}\), small compared with the 2 mV offset. CMRR gets its own skill with differential pairs.

questions.prompt: Preview of transistor speed. The fastest op-amp in the reader's table has GBW = 3.8 GHz. Used at a non-inverting gain of 20, what closed-loop bandwidth would it give, in MHz?
questions.explanation: \(3.8\ \mathrm{GHz}/20=190\ \mathrm{MHz}\). GBW ultimately comes from how fast the internal transistors are; a later skill defines a transistor's own unity-gain frequency \(f_T\), which caps what any op-amp built from it can do.

questions.prompt: Preview of differential pairs. Why does an op-amp datasheet give the input offset as a statistical value of random sign, not a fixed polarity?
options: The manufacturer deliberately adds a random offset
Offset comes from random mismatch between the two nominally identical halves of the input stage (a differential pair), so each part's offset is a different random number
Offset is caused by the power supply polarity
Offset depends only on the signal applied
questions.explanation: The reader explains that offset arises from mismatches between the input differential-pair transistors or load resistors (Sec. 18.2.1). Mismatch is random, so offset is characterized statistically. The differential-pair skills explain the circuit behind this.
